questions.q: What are the four lifecycle states a hosted Claude model moves through, per Anthropic's own documentation?
options: Active, Legacy, Deprecated, Retired
New, Used, Broken, Fixed
Beta, Release, Patch, End-of-life
Free, Paid, Premium, Enterprise
questions.explain: Anthropic's documentation defines the lifecycle as Active (fully supported), Legacy (still works, no updates), Deprecated (not recommended, replacement/date assigned), and Retired (requests fail).

questions.q: What is Anthropic's minimum committed notice period before retiring a publicly released model, per the lesson?
options: No notice is given
Exactly 24 hours
At least 60 days
At least 5 years
questions.explain: Anthropic's documentation commits to at least 60 days' notice before retiring a publicly released model on Anthropic-operated platforms.

questions.q: In the real deprecation case cited in this lesson, what happened to Claude Sonnet 4.5?
options: It was never deprecated and remains active indefinitely
It was retired with zero notice
It was replaced by a model from a different company
Anthropic notified developers on Sept 30, 2026 that it would retire Nov 30, 2026, with Sonnet 5.5 as the recommended replacement
questions.explain: Anthropic's published deprecation history shows Claude Sonnet 4.5 was deprecated Sept 30, 2026, with a Nov 30, 2026 retirement date and Claude Sonnet 5.5 named as the replacement.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend pinning specific, dated model IDs in production code?
options: Because floating to 'whatever is newest' is always cheaper
Because dated model IDs never get deprecated
Because predictability matters, and automatically floating to the newest model risks unexpected behavior changes
Because pinned model IDs are required by law
questions.explain: Pinning a specific, dated model ID gives predictable behavior in production rather than silently changing whenever a provider updates what 'newest' points to.

questions.q: What does the lesson say about the engineering cost of model deprecation?
options: It's a one-time setup cost paid only once, ever
It never requires any engineering work
It only affects open-weight models, never hosted API models
It should be budgeted as an ongoing cost, since models get deprecated on a recurring cadence
questions.explain: Because providers deprecate models on a recurring release cadence, teams using several models over time should expect to budget ongoing engineering time for migrations, not treat it as a one-time cost.
